cases.abstract: DROID addresses the challenge of collecting manipulation demonstrations across varied scenes while retaining a reproducible robot control setup. We present a distributed manipulation dataset and portable collection platform shared by 13 institutions. Common Franka Panda hardware supports reproducible collection across sites, while camera calibration, scene-specific task sampling and periodic environment changes are used to broaden coverage. The dataset contains 76,000 successful episodes; the collection spans 564 scenes and 350 hours. Hardware and software instructions, visualization tools and policy-training resources accompany the release. We evaluate the data using existing language-conditioned diffusion policies on six tasks in four locations, all with DROID hardware. We compare in-domain-only training against equal mixtures of in-domain demonstrations with either successful DROID trajectories or a curated Open X-Embodiment mixture, holding the policy backbone fixed. With ten rollouts per method and task setting, DROID co-training exceeds the next-best method in across-task mean success rate by 22 percentage points in-distribution and 17 on task-specific out-of-distribution variants. These results support supplementary training with DROID for the evaluated tasks and scene changes.
cases.methods: DROID uses shared Franka Panda hardware to keep robot control reproducible across collection sites while a portable platform enables scene changes. Collectors operate through VR teleoperation with two adjustable external stereo cameras and a wrist stereo camera. For each scene, they position and calibrate cameras and enter feasible tasks. Random assignment selects the task for each episode, while periodic prompts encourage changes in camera placement, lighting, clutter or base position. To evaluate successful DROID trajectories as supplementary training data, we train separate language-conditioned diffusion policies for six tasks across four locations on DROID hardware. With the same backbone, we compare in-domain-only training with equal mixtures of in-domain demonstrations and either DROID trajectories or curated Open X-Embodiment data. Ten rollouts per method and task setting cover perturbed robot and object positions in-distribution and task-specific out-of-distribution variants.
cases.results: Across the six evaluated tasks, DROID co-training achieves a higher mean success rate than in-domain-only training or co-training with curated Open X-Embodiment data. All methods use the same diffusion-policy backbone, and both co-training regimes mix supplementary trajectories equally with in-domain demonstrations. With ten rollouts per method and task setting on DROID hardware, DROID co-training exceeds the next-best method by 22 percentage points in-distribution and 17 on task-specific out-of-distribution variants. Error bars report standard errors around the across-task mean success rates. A size-matched comparison examines scene coverage: with 7,362 successful demonstrations per subset and 50/50 in-domain co-training, the uniformly sampled, more scene-diverse subset outperforms the subset from the 20 most represented scenes on the challenging out-of-distribution tasks studied. This comparison supports a role for scene diversity beyond subset size, without isolating it from all other differences.

notes.abstract: Plan: retain data and collection-platform contributions, connect common hardware to scene variation, and evaluate supplementary-data utility (D01-D07, D09). Read-back: the prose specifies successful episodes, shared-backbone comparators, task averages and evaluated scene shifts; it does not promise a new policy algorithm.
notes.methods: Plan: explain how collectors generate varied episodes before defining the shared-backbone comparison (D01-D02, D05-D07). Read-back: task assignment and variation prompts have explicit roles; training mixtures and rollout settings remain distinct. Coverage is an intended collection function, not an isolated experimental cause.
notes.results: Plan: compare training-data regimes, then distinguish diversity from subset size (D06-D08). Read-back: the success-rate margins concern six-task averages; standard errors describe those means, not the margins. The subset experiment retains its own scope and does not establish an isolated diversity effect.

cases.abstract: We introduce SIMPLER, a simulated evaluation framework for comparing policies trained on real robot data despite discrepancies in control and appearance. Its target is relative performance, not exact reproduction of real-world success rates. Existing demonstration actions are replayed to tune simulated controllers against real end-effector motion. Visual Matching composites segmented simulated robots and interactive objects onto an inpainted real background and adjusts textures to align their appearance. Mean Maximum Rank Violation (MMRV) averages each policy's largest real-world success-rate margin involved in a simulator misranking; lower values indicate better ranking agreement. Across six policy checkpoints and three Google Robot task groups, Visual Matching yields average MMRV of 0.056, compared with 0.143 for Variant Aggregation, which averages outcomes across randomized visual variants, and 0.375 for rankings based on validation action mean squared error. WidowX comparisons yield task-averaged MMRV of 0.014. These results support relative policy evaluation in the tested, mainly rigid-body setups, while some checkpoints remain sensitive to visual differences. The open-source release provides environments and construction guidance for reuse.
cases.methods: SIMPLER constructs SAPIEN evaluations for Google Robot and WidowX policies trained on real data, focusing mainly on rigid-body tasks. System identification first replays actions from existing real demonstrations and compares simulated and real end-effector translation and rotation. Simulated annealing adjusts controller stiffness and damping to reduce this mismatch, aligning action effects without training a replacement policy. Visual Matching then composites segmented simulated robots and interactive objects onto an inpainted real background and adjusts or projects textures. Variant Aggregation provides an alternative by averaging evaluation outcomes across randomized visual variants. Paired real and simulated evaluations assess policy-ranking agreement. Mean Maximum Rank Violation averages, across policies, each policy's largest real-world success-rate margin involved in a simulator misranking; lower values indicate better agreement. Pearson correlation separately measures linear association, which need not capture ranking fidelity.
cases.results: Visual Matching tracks real-world policy ordering more closely than Variant Aggregation or rankings based on validation action mean squared error across six policy checkpoints and three Google Robot task groups. Average Mean Maximum Rank Violation, which penalizes reversals by their real-world success-rate margins, is 0.056 for Visual Matching, versus 0.143 and 0.375 for the alternatives, respectively; lower values indicate closer ranking agreement. Mean Pearson correlations are 0.924, 0.778 and 0.308 in the same order. The comparison supports visually matched simulation as a better ranking signal in these task groups than either variant averaging or validation action error. A secondary check tests a behavioral prediction: simulation suggests that Octo-Base is more sensitive to arm texture than RT-1-X, and real-world arm-wrapping experiments support this relative sensitivity. Thus, the agreement extends to a specific visual robustness pattern, not to exact success-rate reproduction for every policy or task.

notes.abstract: Plan: preserve framework, gap-alignment operations, ranking metric and reusable environments (S01-S05, S07-S08, S10). Read-back: MMRV is defined before its comparisons; Google Robot and WidowX evidence concerns ranking agreement in tested setups, with visual sensitivity retained as a consequential exception.
notes.methods: Plan: connect controller calibration and image construction to paired ranking evaluation (S02-S06). Read-back: demonstration replay aligns action effects without replacing the policy; Visual Matching and Variant Aggregation have different visual operations. MMRV and Pearson correlation measure related but noninterchangeable constructs.
notes.results: Plan: interpret agreement metrics, then check relative texture sensitivity against hardware (S07, S09). Read-back: the averages belong to the Google Robot task-group comparison, not robot success rates; arm wrapping supports a specific simulated sensitivity contrast, not universal simulation fidelity (S01, S10).
